guideTitle: Best Paper Shredders for Staples and Paper Clips (2026)
metaTitle: Best Shredders for Staples and Paper Clips
metaDescription: Six shredders that accept staples and paper clips, compared on how they handle metal fasteners, cut size, run time and bin size so you can skip the pre-sorting.
expertTake: The Amazon Basics 15-sheet cross-cut is the best staple-friendly shredder because it takes staples and small clips straight from the stack with a roomy 6-gallon bin. The Bonsaii 9-sheet is the value pick for a household that wants staple tolerance in a small body. Skip all of these if your paper is bound with heavy binder clips or large fasteners, since those need to be removed by hand regardless.
introParagraphs: Pulling staples is the most boring chore in paper shredding, and it is also the reason many people give up and bin their documents whole. A shredder that accepts fasteners saves real time, but the claim hides important limits about how many staples, what size and in which mode.

Hardened steel in a staple is tougher than the paper around it, so cutters wear faster when fasteners go through. The good machines use stronger cutters and a clean cut type, while the cheap ones accept a staple but pay for it in dull blades. Knowing what a machine really accepts is the first step to buying well.

products.name: Amazon Basics 15-Sheet Cross-Cut Shredder, 6 Gal, Staples OK
products.description:
Sorting staples out of a stack of paperwork is exactly the job this machine removes. The listing states that 15 sheets of 20 lb paper go through at once, staples and small paper clips included, which makes it the clearest on-the-record answer to the fastener question in this guide.

The cutters produce pieces of about 5.1 by 25.4 millimetres at P-4, a sensible level for household records. The entry is 8.7 inches wide, so a letter page feeds without folding. CDs, DVDs and cards go through a dedicated slot, which keeps the plastic away from the paper feed and lets the main cutter focus on sheets and fasteners.

Ownership comes down to cutter wear. Staples are steel, so each one adds a tiny amount of wear, and the cutters will not last forever if you feed staple-heavy stacks daily. A 6-gallon wastebasket holds the confetti comfortably. Choose it over the Bonsaii 9-sheet if your stacks regularly reach 12 pages with staples attached.
products.bestFor: Households that want to drop stapled documents straight into the slot.
pros: Explicitly accepts staples and small clips
Dedicated slot for CDs and cards
cons: Cutters wear faster with heavy staple use
Long strips are less secure than micro-cut

products.name: Bonsaii 12-Sheet Micro-Cut Shredder with Clips, Staples, 5.5 Gal
products.description:
This model lists cards, paper clips and staples among the things it takes, and it does so with a micro-cut head. That is a harder combination than it sounds, because tiny cutting teeth meet steel more often and wear faster than coarser cross-cut teeth.

A patented cooling system allows five minutes of continuous running. That is shorter than the 6 minutes you get on some cross-cut siblings, but adequate for a stapled stack of a few dozen pages. The 5.5-gallon bin holds about 350 sheets of A4, so it will handle a good session before it asks to be emptied.

Over several years, expect to oil the cutters and keep fasteners to a reasonable number per stack. The fine particles are the reward: a stapled bank statement ends up as dust. Compared with the Amazon Basics 15-sheet, you trade three sheets of capacity and some speed for a finer cut. Pick it for security first and convenience second.
products.bestFor: People who staple sensitive paperwork and want fine particles.
pros: Cooling system supports a five-minute run
cons: Three fewer sheets than the 15-sheet pick

products.name: Bonsaii 9-Sheet Cross-Cut Shredder for Home, Staples and Clips
products.description:
Built for a spare room, this is a P-4 cross-cut unit with pieces of about 5 by 18 millimetres, shorter than the long strips on the Amazon Basics 15-sheet. It lists staples and clips among the things it can handle and gives a clear claim for output: about 180 sheets in one five-minute run, then a 40-minute cooldown.

The 40-minute rest is long, so this is a machine for a single batch, not a marathon. The nine-sheet head means a stapled pack of about eight pages is its comfortable limit. It is also lighter and smaller than the bigger units here, which makes it easier to store between uses.

In practice, treat the staple tolerance as an allowance, not an invitation. One staple per packet is fine, and a stack with clusters of fasteners will wear the cutters. It sits in a lower price tier than the micro-cut model, so it fits a household that wants a tidy, affordable, general-purpose shredder.
products.bestFor: Small households shredding a modest stack of stapled mail.
pros: Shorter 5 x 18 mm pieces for better security
Light body is easy to store
cons: Nine sheets is the limit for stapled packs

products.name: Aurora AU1210MA 12-Sheet Micro-Cut Shredder with Small Clips
products.description:
Stapled paperwork piles up in offices, and this Aurora is built for the long haul with a 60-minute run time. It destroys small paper clips, CDs, DVDs and credit cards, with a micro-cut particle of about 5/32 by 15/32 inch at P-4.

The small print matters: the listing names small paper clips, so be careful with heavy-duty clips and large binder clips. The 12-sheet head works for stapled packs, and a basket of about 300 sheets stops you from emptying too often during a long job.

It is the most office-oriented machine here, which shows in the price tier and the commitment to an hour of continuous run. If you shred on weekends in big batches, this is a serious tool. The trade is that it is a slower, fine-cut machine, so it moves fewer sheets per minute than the 15-sheet cross-cut. For a staple-heavy workload, make sure to keep cutters oiled per the manual.
products.bestFor: Offices that shred stapled paperwork for an hour at a time.
pros: Destroys small clips, CDs, DVDs and cards

products.name: Locksworth 110-Sheet Auto Feed Micro-Cut Shredder, 6.9 Gal
products.description:
Auto-feed shredders and fasteners are an awkward mix, and this Locksworth is honest about it. The listing says auto mode shreds paper only, so staples and clips go through manual mode instead. That is the correct design, because a tray that cannot see a staple will happily feed it into the cutter.

In auto mode the machine takes up to 110 sheets and runs for 60 minutes, which suits a long job of unstapled paper. The P-4 micro-cut head turns pages into tiny pieces, and the 6.9-gallon bin has a window and casters for easy emptying.

Plan on a two-step workflow. Pull staples from bulk stacks and load the tray, then use manual mode for the occasional stapled packet. If you rarely have staples, the auto tray is a time saver. If you have them constantly, the Amazon Basics 15-sheet is a simpler fit because it takes staples straight from a manual slot with no sorting.
products.bestFor: Large paper piles where only a few packets carry fasteners.
pros: 6.9-gallon bin has casters and a window

products.name: Bonsaii 6-Sheet Cross-Cut Shredder with Staples, 3.4 Gal Bin
products.description:
The cheapest tier in the guide still lists staples and credit cards among the items it shreds. Particles measure about 5 by 14 millimetres at P-4, which sits between the cuts on the Bonsaii 9-sheet and the Amazon Basics 15-sheet.

Its four-minute run and 20-minute cooldown are modest but the rest period is the shortest here. A handle on the head helps lifting, and the 3.4-gallon bin has a clear window so you can see when it is time to empty. The six-sheet head is small, so a stapled pack of five pages is the practical maximum.

This is the machine for a few documents a week. Do not expect it to digest big stapled bundles, and keep the stack well under its rating when metal is present. For a household that wants a basic staple-tolerant unit under the desk, it is enough. Spend up to the Bonsaii 9-sheet if your packs run longer.
products.bestFor: Light use where a few stapled sheets need to disappear.
pros: Rests only 20 minutes after a run
Handle makes lifting the head easy
cons: Six sheets is a small stack

buyingCriteria.explanation: Some machines accept staples in the main slot, others only in a manual mode. The Amazon Basics 15-sheet takes staples and small clips directly, while the Locksworth 110-sheet auto tray takes paper only. Read where the fasteners go before you buy, because a tray that rejects them reintroduces the pre-sorting chore.

Staples and small paper clips are one thing; heavy binder clips, fold-back clips and paper-clip chains are another. The Aurora AU1210MA names small paper clips specifically, and the Bonsaii models list staples and clips without a size. Remove anything bigger than a standard clip by hand.

Steel wears cutters faster than paper does. A micro-cut head like the Bonsaii 12-sheet has more cutting edges meeting each staple than a cross-cut head like the Bonsaii 9-sheet. Expect shorter blade life if you feed staples daily, and oil the cutters more often.

Cross-cut handles fasteners with less strain, while micro-cut gives finer fragments. The Amazon Basics 15-sheet leaves 5.1 by 25.4 mm strips, the Bonsaii 9-sheet 5 by 18 mm, and the Aurora about 5/32 by 15/32 inch. Match the cut to the sensitivity of the paper, not just the staple load.

Rated capacity assumes clean paper. A stapled packet counts as thicker, so derate by 2 to 4 sheets. A 9-sheet Bonsaii handles about 6 to 7 stapled pages in practice, while a 15-sheet unit handles 11 to 13.

Stapled batches take longer because you feed fewer sheets per pass. The Aurora runs 60 minutes with a 300-sheet basket, while the Bonsaii 6-sheet runs 4 minutes with a 3.4-gallon bin. For big batches pick the longer cycle.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fastener policy
howWeEvaluated.description: We read what each machine says about staples and clips, noting where they must be fed. The Amazon Basics 15-sheet and Bonsaii models are explicit. The Locksworth routes fasteners to manual mode and the Aurora names small clips only.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cutter strain
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cut type and teeth density to judge likely wear. Cross-cut units strain less than micro-cut. The Aurora AU1210MA and Bonsaii 12-sheet micro-cut get extra credit for staying in service despite finer teeth.

howWeEvaluated.title: Practical capacity
howWeEvaluated.description: We derated sheet counts for stapled packets, since fasteners add thickness. A 15-sheet unit behaves like a 12-sheet one on stapled stacks. This is based on spec sheets and owner feedback patterns.

howWeEvaluated.title: Session length
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared run time and cooldown, from 4 minutes on the Bonsaii 6-sheet to 60 on the Aurora and Locksworth. Stapled loads feed more slowly, so longer cycles help.

howWeEvaluated.title: Ownership
howWeEvaluated.description: We considered bin size, casters and windows, and the upkeep of oiling cutters. The Locksworth's wheeled 6.9-gallon bin and the Amazon Basics 6-gallon basket reduce emptying effort.

faq.a: No. Some accept them in the main slot, others only in manual mode, and a few do not at all. Check the listing and the manual before feeding. If the wording only says the machine shreds paper, assume fasteners are not welcome, because a quiet listing usually means the maker did not design or rate the cutters for metal.

Over time they dull them. Cross-cut cutters handle staples better than micro-cut, but all steel shortens blade life. Oil the cutters and avoid heavy clusters. Spreading staples across several passes rather than feeding a thick packet with a metal-heavy corner is the simplest way to keep blade life long.

Not in most machines. Small paper clips are commonly accepted, while binder clips and large fasteners should be removed. Spiral bindings, plastic combs and metal rings are also best taken off first, since they are thicker than anything the cutters are sized for.

faq.q: How many stapled pages can I feed?
faq.a: Take 2 to 4 sheets off the rating. A 15-sheet unit handles about 11 to 13 stapled pages.

faq.q: Is micro-cut or cross-cut better with staples?
faq.a: Cross-cut strains less. Micro-cut gives finer pieces but wears faster. Choose by what the paper contains. A household that mostly shreds stapled utility bills can stay with cross-cut, while someone destroying tax files with a staple in every corner should accept the extra wear of micro-cut for the finer result.

faq.q: Is it safe to feed staples through the auto tray?
faq.a: Only if the manual says so. Some auto trays are paper only, such as the Locksworth, and fasteners go in manual mode. Treat that rule as a feature, since it keeps hard metal away from a tray that runs unattended for an hour.
